title: Definiteness, description & possession
scope: Selected existing cards from Books 1 and 3A; not exhaustive topic coverage.
externalPrerequisites: Recognize basic masculine/feminine and singular/plural distinctions.
Recognize simple nominal sentences and common prepositions; source cards provide supporting context.

concepts.title: Recognize an indefinite noun
concepts.rule: For ordinary nouns such as كِتَابٌ, tanwin accompanies an indefinite meaning: “a book.”
concepts.note: An introductory pattern, not a definition of every word with tanwin.

sourceCards.title: Where is the word “a”?
sourceCards.takeaway: For these nouns, the ending helps express “a” or “an.”

examples.translation: A book · a house · a mosque

reviewPrompts.prompt: What does كِتَابٌ mean in this example?

concepts.title: Make a noun definite with الـ
concepts.rule: Add الـ and remove tanwin: بَيْتٌ becomes الْبَيْتُ.
concepts.note: The example is nominative; الـ does not determine the noun’s case.

sourceCards.title: Make “a house” into “the house”
sourceCards.takeaway: Add الـ and remove tanwin: a noun becomes definite.

examples.translation: A house → the house

reviewPrompts.answer: الْبَيْتُ. Add الـ and replace tanwin with the appropriate single case vowel.

concepts.title: Put the adjective after its noun
concepts.rule: In a describing phrase, place the noun before its adjective: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ, “a new house.”
concepts.note: This is a phrase; a predicate makes a statement.

sourceCards.title: Put the describing word after the noun
sourceCards.takeaway: For “a new house,” say “a house, new”: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ.

examples.translation: A new house

reviewPrompts.prompt: Say “a new house” using بَيْتٌ and جَدِيدٌ.

concepts.title: Match the noun’s grammatical gender
concepts.rule: A describing adjective agrees with its noun in grammatical gender, even when the noun has no ة.
concepts.note: Assumes basic recognition of masculine and feminine nouns.

sourceCards.title: Match the adjective to the noun’s gender
sourceCards.takeaway: Match grammatical gender, rather than just copying the noun’s last letter.

examples.arabic:
وَلَدٌ صَغِيرٌ   ·   بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ
كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ   ·   سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ
examples.translation:
A small boy · a small girl
A new book · a new car

reviewPrompts.prompt: Choose: بِنْتٌ صَغِيرٌ or بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ?
reviewPrompts.answer: بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ. بِنْتٌ is feminine although it has no ة.

concepts.title: Match definiteness in a describing phrase
concepts.rule: For an ordinary noun made definite with الـ, its describing adjective takes الـ too.
concepts.note: Nouns can also be definite without الـ; possessed nouns appear later in the path.

sourceCards.title: Match “the” on the adjective too
sourceCards.takeaway: For “the new teacher,” both the noun and its describing adjective take الـ.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.

concepts.title: Distinguish a description from a statement
concepts.rule: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ means “the new teacher”; الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ means “the teacher is new.”
concepts.note: A comparison assembled from two cards, not a claim that the cards are duplicates. These examples do not make every predicate indefinite.

sourceCards.title: Match “the” on the adjective too
sourceCards.takeaway: For “the new teacher,” both the noun and its describing adjective take الـ.

sourceCards.title: Tanwin does not always mean “a”
sourceCards.takeaway: On these describing words, tanwin does not add an English “a.”

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.

The door is open.
The pen is broken.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Which is a statement: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ or الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ?
reviewPrompts.answer: الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: “The teacher is new.” The indefinite word is the predicate here.

concepts.title: Do not translate every tanwin as “a”
concepts.rule: Tanwin is an ending, not an English word: مَفْتُوحٌ in this predicate means “open,” not “a open.”
concepts.note: Retained as a qualification of the introductory tanwin pattern.

sourceCards.title: Tanwin does not always mean “a”
sourceCards.takeaway: On these describing words, tanwin does not add an English “a.”

examples.translation:
The door is open.
The pen is broken.

concepts.title: A name can be definite and have tanwin
concepts.rule: A proper name such as حَامِدٌ identifies a person and is definite even though it has tanwin.
concepts.note: Separate from predicate translation: this addresses definiteness itself.

sourceCards.title: A name can have tanwin too
sourceCards.takeaway: Translate the name itself; do not add “a” because of tanwin.

examples.translation: Hamid

reviewPrompts.prompt: Does حَامِدٌ mean “a Hamid” because it has tanwin?
reviewPrompts.answer: No. It is the name Hamid; a proper name is definite.

concepts.title: Put the thing before its owner
concepts.rule: In an ordinary possessive idafah, put the thing first and the owner second: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ.
concepts.note: Mudaf = first noun; mudaf ilayhi = complement. Idafah can express relationships beyond ownership.

sourceCards.title: Put the thing before its owner
sourceCards.takeaway: Thing first, owner second: “book of Bilal.”

examples.translation:
Bilal’s book
The imam’s house

reviewPrompts.prompt: Say “Bilal’s book” using كِتَاب and بِلَال.
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ: thing first, owner second.

concepts.title: Leave الـ and tanwin off the first noun
concepts.rule: In the ordinary possessive idafah taught here, the first noun has neither الـ nor tanwin.
concepts.note: Missing tanwin alone does not prove that the phrase is definite.

sourceCards.title: The first word loses الـ and tanwin
sourceCards.takeaway: In كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ, leave both الـ and tanwin off كِتَابُ.

examples.translation: Bilal’s book

reviewPrompts.prompt: Correct كِتَابٌ بِلَالٍ to mean “Bilal’s book.”
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ. Remove tanwin from the first noun.

concepts.title: Give the complement its majrur role
concepts.rule: The second part of an idafah is majrur. Ordinary declinable nouns show kasrah, with or without tanwin.
concepts.note: Case is a grammatical role; not every word shows it with kasrah.

sourceCards.title: The owner takes a majrur ending
sourceCards.takeaway: Look for “i” or “in” on the owner in these examples.

examples.translation:
Bilal’s house
The imam’s house

reviewPrompts.prompt: Why is بِلَالٍ majrur in كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ?
reviewPrompts.answer: It is the mudaf ilayhi, the second part of the idafah.

concepts.title: Match the adjective’s case to its noun
concepts.rule: A describing adjective takes the case of the noun it describes. In longer phrases, use this to identify which noun is described.
concepts.note: One shared case-agreement rule. The later card is retained as an advanced application, with its own example. Basic preposition knowledge helps with the first example.

sourceCards.title: The adjective follows the noun’s case
sourceCards.takeaway: When the noun becomes majrur, its describing adjective becomes majrur too.

sourceCards.title: The ending tells you what is new
sourceCards.takeaway: Match the adjective’s case to the noun it describes.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ
أَنَا فِي بَيْتٍ جَدِيدٍ
مَنْ فِي الْبَيْتِ الْجَدِيدِ؟
examples.translation:
This is a new house.
I am in a new house.
Who is in the new house?

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدُ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدِ
examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
The new imam’s house

reviewPrompts.prompt: In بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدِ, is the house or the imam new?
reviewPrompts.answer: The imam. الْجَدِيدِ agrees with majrur الْإِمَامِ. With الْجَدِيدُ, the house is new.

concepts.title: Attach “your,” “his,” and “her”
concepts.rule: Attached pronouns can fill the owner’s place: كِتَابُكَ, كِتَابُهُ, كِتَابُهَا. The first noun has no الـ or tanwin.
concepts.note: ـكَ addresses one male person; ـهُ is “his” and ـهَا is “her.”

sourceCards.title: Attach “your,” “his,” and “her” to the noun
sourceCards.takeaway: Attach the owner: كِتَابُ + ـكَ becomes كِتَابُكَ.

examples.translation: Your book (one male person) · his book · her book

concepts.title: Use the long ī ending for “my”
concepts.rule: كِتَابِي means “my book.” Read a long final ī rather than the u heard before some other owner endings.
concepts.note: Kept separately because this form adds a pronunciation distinction.

sourceCards.title: A long “ī” for “my”
sourceCards.takeaway: كِتَابِي means “my book,” with a long final “ī.”

examples.translation: My book

reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابِي, with a long final ī.

concepts.title: Check what the idafah is linked to
concepts.rule: In these ordinary idafahs, a definite complement makes the phrase definite; an indefinite complement leaves it indefinite.
concepts.note: A later refinement, not a duplicate of the introductory possession cards.

sourceCards.title: Idafah takes definiteness from its complement
sourceCards.takeaway: Check the complement, not just the mudaf’s missing tanwin.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابُ هَذَا · كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ · كِتَابُهُ · كِتَابُ حَامِدٍ
كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ · بَيْتُ مُدَرِّسٍ
examples.translation:
This person’s book · the teacher’s book · his book · Hamid’s book
A student’s book · a teacher’s house

reviewPrompts.prompt: Compare كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ and كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ. Which is definite?
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ is definite (“the teacher’s book”). كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ is indefinite (“a student’s book”). Both first nouns lack tanwin.

concepts.title: Finish the idafah before describing the first noun
concepts.rule: An adjective describing the first noun follows the complete idafah. In the definite examples here, that adjective is definite.
concepts.note: Use adjective-case to distinguish description of the thing from description of its owner.

sourceCards.title: Describe a possessed thing after the whole phrase
sourceCards.takeaway: Complete the possession phrase first, then add the first noun’s adjective.

examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
His new house

concepts.title: Recognize several ways of being definite
concepts.rule: Personal pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and nouns with الـ are definite categories in this source.
concepts.note: An overview of the categories listed on this card, not an exhaustive account of every construction. Relative pronouns can be explored through the source card.

sourceCards.title: Definite nouns identify something specific
sourceCards.takeaway: Definiteness is not the same as having الْـ or lacking tanwin.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا · أَنْتَ · هُوَ
أَحْمَدُ · بِلَالٌ · مَكَّةُ
هَذَا · ذَلِكَ · أُولَئِكَ
الَّذِي · الَّذِينَ · الَّتِي
الْكِتَابُ · الرَّجُلُ
examples.translation:
I · you · he
Ahmad · Bilal · Makkah
This · that · those
Relative pronouns: who/which
The book · the man

reviewPrompts.prompt: Must every definite word begin with الـ? Give a counterexample.
reviewPrompts.answer: No. For example, حَامِدٌ is a definite proper name; أَنَا is a definite personal pronoun.

concepts.title: Track each noun’s reason for its ending
concepts.rule: In عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ, the first noun is majrur after عَلَى; the second is majrur as the idafah complement.
concepts.note: Assumes recognition of عَلَى as a preposition.

sourceCards.title: Two reasons for two “i” endings
sourceCards.takeaway: The first noun follows the preposition; the second follows the possession rule.

examples.translation: On the teacher’s table

reviewPrompts.prompt: Why do both nouns have kasrah in عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ?
reviewPrompts.answer: مَكْتَبِ follows عَلَى; الْمُدَرِّسِ is the mudaf ilayhi. The first noun’s own case can change.

concepts.title: Extend agreement to non-human plurals
concepts.rule: In the basic rule taught here, non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ.
concepts.note: Two complementary steps—recognize the class, then apply its agreement. Assumes basic singular/plural recognition; exceptions remain outside this pilot.

sourceCards.title: People and non-human plurals behave differently
sourceCards.takeaway: Identify whether the plural refers to people or to non-human things.

sourceCards.title: Treat non-human plurals as feminine singular
sourceCards.takeaway: Non-human plural meaning can take feminine singular Arabic agreement.

examples.translation: These are new students; they are small.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ، هُوَ صَغِيرٌ
هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ، هِيَ صَغِيرَةٌ
examples.translation:
This is a new book; it is small.
These are new books; they are small.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Choose: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدٌ, كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ, or كُتُبٌ جُدُدٌ for the basic rule here.
reviewPrompts.answer: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ. كُتُبٌ is a non-human plural; its adjective is feminine singular.
